question: What is the nature of the detailed information held by the Gang Harm Insights Centre, and does it include breakdown of convictions, charges, and active membership by gang?
reply:
I am advised that the Gang Harm Insights Centre (GHIC) is a multi-agency strategic insights group which actively partners to deliver holistic, actionable, and timely insights, enabling agencies to empower communities in making a difference to gang-related harm. The GHIC seeks to provide a holistic understanding of the harm caused by, to, and within the gang environment by looking at the drivers behind harmful behaviour, working with community members to have their voice at the centre of the work, and incorporating partner agency information.

The GHIC has an Approved Information Sharing Agreement (AISA) between the 12 agencies which authorises the sharing of information about gangs and gang-related harm, enabling agencies to take steps to reduce this harm. The intent is not to enable broad bilateral information sharing between the parties, rather to provide legal authority for highly managed information sharing and insights generation with the GHIC at the centre of all information flows.

The GHIC does not hold information on convictions and charges by gang, but this information can be readily retrieved through the AISA mechanism. Gang membership is held by Police, however the GHIC takes an active role in ensuring quality of this information and continuous improvement of the established processes.

question: What progress, if any, has been made in the quarter October to December 2024 in the priority area ‘Build sector knowledge, research and statistical information to improve sexual health outcomes for Māori and improve equity’ ‘STRATEGIC DIRECTION 1: Surveillance, information and public health knowledge systems to drive action’ as part of the Aotearoa New Zealand Sexually Transmitted and Blood Borne Infection Strategy 2023-2030?
reply: I refer the Member to Written Parliamentary Question 15495 (2025).
referred_reply:
Published in March 2023, the Sexually Transmitted and Blood Borne Infections (STBBI) Strategy sets out a roadmap to 2030 to achieve an Aotearoa New Zealand where STBBI are prevented and where all people living with STBBI live long and healthy lives free from stigma and discrimination.
 
 Officials from across the Ministry of Health (the Ministry) and Health NZ have developed a cross-agency STBBI work programme to implement the STBBI Strategy with an initial focus on the HIV, hepatitis C and syphilis action plans that sit under it, as well as hepatitis B and contracts with other STBBI related non-governmental and community organisations such as the Needle Exchange Programme (NEP).

 The goals and objectives in the strategy are intentionally high-level and the Ministry expects activities being taken to deliver on the priority action plans noted above to contribute to these over time.
 
 Specifically in the quarter October to December 2024, the following activities were progressed, all of which contribute towards implementing the strategic approaches for the STBBI Strategy.
 
 • There continued to be a strong focus on connecting with refugee migrants and asylum seeker groups, Hauora Māori partners, needle exchange services and sex workers to support these communities to be able to deliver future HIV and sexually transmitted infection (STI) testing.
 • Procurement documents were completed to expand innovative HIV and STI testing services to priority populations. A request for proposal will commence in quarter three 2024/25.
 • A working group, primarily involving people living with HIV representing the priority population groups, completed community engagement to test key concepts and gather insights on HIV stigma. This will inform development of an HIV campaign to challenge stigma and discrimination.
 • In response to the increase in HIV cases in Fiji, officials presented to the heads of Public Service Agencies in Fiji to provide insight on the management of HIV in New Zealand. Health NZ is also working with stakeholders to raise awareness of HIV amongst the Pacific population in New Zealand and increase HIV and STI testing.
 • Training, endorsed by the Nursing Council and the Pharmacy Council, continued to be promoted for nurses and pharmacists to provide hepatitis C treatment without prescription. 
• The HIV Monitoring Plan was published in June 2024 to support and measure progress towards achieving the goals and targets of the HIV Action Plan. Work is underway to develop the first HIV Monitoring Report. This report is expected to be delivered mid-2025.
 • Work to develop a teaching package for midwives on syphilis and other STIs has progressed with consultation with subject matter experts. The New Zealand College of Midwives is working in collaboration with Ngā Maia Māori Midwives Aotearoa and Pacific Midwives Aotearoa/Moana Connect to deliver the training.
 • Work commenced on preparations for procurement to identify a provider to develop a national campaign to raise awareness of syphilis and promote testing in sexually active heterosexual people. The campaign aims to address the increasing rates of syphilis in New Zealand and the associated cases of babies being born with congenital syphilis.

question: What progress, if any, has been made in the quarter April to June 2024 in actioning the recommendation ‘Strengthening primary care accountability regarding Te Tiriti o Waitangi obligations to Māori, and equity obligations, by proactively facilitating mana-enhancing early engagement with families to achieve timely 6-week vaccinations and ongoing access for health checks’ under ‘Priority Area 4: Enrolment into health services from birth’ within the ‘Initial Priorities for the National Immunisation Programme in Aotearoa 2022’?
reply:
I am advised that this recommendation has been completed. 

I refer the Member to my response to Written Parliamentary Question 53916 and 74166 (2024).
referred_reply:
I am advised that during the January to March 2024 quarter, the pre-call/recall initiative in general practice was under development. The service includes Primary Health Organisations (PHO) funding for six-week immunisations and for focusing on improving outcomes for Māori. Additional funding has been targeted at achieving six-week immunisation of Māori children and to help Māori PHOs drive immunisation coordination functions. 
I am further advised that as part of the PHO annual uplift process, the PHO agreement has been amended to explicitly state that there is no requirement to sight a birth certificate to enroll an infant, and to extend provisional enrolment for up to 12 months.

question: What engagement, if any, took place with Te Taura Whiri, organisations before releasing a proposal to make teaching of te reo Māori a downgrade from being a primary objective in the Education and Training Act?
reply: I refer the Member to my response to written parliamentary question 58139 (2024).
referred_reply:
There is no intention to downgrade the teaching of te reo Māori that forms part of Te Tiriti o Waitangi objective in section 127 of the Education and Training Act (the Act) 2020. Public consultation on the proposals to amend section 127 of the Act are currently taking place, which includes consultation with Māori education organisations. No consultation with Te Taura Whiri, iwi, hapū or Māori education organisations took place before the proposals were released for public consultation.

On 7 June 2024, I received a report titled Amendments to section 127 of the Education and Training Act 2020. 

This is also my response to written parliamentary questions 58141, 58143, 58144, 58145 (2024).
